product_scope: Foodvisor's photo feature is intended to identify multiple visible foods in a meal and return an editable food log with calories, macronutrients, vitamins, and minerals. Premium is required for photo meal analysis; the free tier emphasizes manual logging. Support recommends a top-down, bright photo with foods separated and allows selecting an alternative, searching manually, or omitting a wrong suggestion. Historical technical reporting described food classification plus estimated weight from plate and phone geometry. recognition_behavior: The public flow is Photo tab, capture or select an image, backend analysis, candidate foods and nutrition, user confirmation or correction, then meal logging. Foodvisor recommends a top-down, bright image with foods separated; when a food is missed or mismatched, the user can choose an alternative, search manually, return to the photo, or omit the suggestion. Static analysis of Android 7.2.0 maps the current multimodal path to a multipart POST at food/search/multimodal/ with image and payload parts, returning response_type, conversation_id, and an optional food or error. Separate routes accept a food-report photo and nutrition-table photo, and a choice endpoint records corrections. This is a current client request shape from static analysis, not a live UI or network trace. portion_and_nutrition_method: Historical public reporting says Foodvisor used autofocus data to estimate plate-to-phone distance, measured the image area of each food, extrapolated volume using food-specific assumptions, and estimated weight; the user could correct the result before logging. Current Android DTOs expose analysis confidence, main_food_id, quantity, food_id, unit_id, and FoodInfoRemote records with per-100g calories, proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, fiber, micronutrients, g_per_serving, food units, barcode, brand, and database-source fields. This supports a vision quantity to Foodvisor food-database and nutrition-unit mapping, with manual correction and a separate nutrition-label OCR path for packaged foods. The current portion formula, hidden-ingredient handling, density assumptions, and calibration are not disclosed; the terms state that results are indicative and accuracy is not guaranteed. reverse_engineering_limits: This was static inspection of one public Android 7.2.0 XAPK only. The app was not installed or executed; no authenticated account, paid feature, food photo upload, runtime API response, TLS traffic capture, or server-side experiment was used; the iOS binary was not inspected. R8 obfuscation, split packaging, remote configuration, downloaded models, feature flags, and backend changes can hide or change behavior. The API path template was found, but the runtime-resolved version and platform path were not observed. Absence of a model asset does not prove cloud-only inference, and the save_gpt_food name does not prove an OpenAI or other named provider. Historical portion claims may not describe the current model. The checked privacy policy does not state a precise raw food-photo retention period. No attempt was made to bypass authentication, DRM, or transport security.
candidate_models: Candidates for SuperNutrition, not evidence of Foodvisor's model: MobileNetV3-small or large as a food-specific classifier backbone; EfficientDet-Lite or another small detector for multiple food regions; MobileNet- or DeepLab-style segmentation for portion masks; and a small ONNX detector such as a YOLO variant only after license review. Use food-specific training or fine-tuning rather than generic ImageNet labels, and evaluate Food-101, FoodSeg103, Nutrition5k, or an internally consented meal set as appropriate. MediaPipe Tasks accepts compatible TFLite model assets for Android; ONNX Runtime Mobile accepts ONNX models; ExecuTorch is an option for exported PyTorch vision models or small multimodal models. Ultralytics code is AGPL-3.0 or commercial, while MediaPipe is Apache 2.0; verify the exact weights, dataset, and model license before shipping. None of these models is a validated calorie or portion estimator by itself. mobile_runtime_support: Android options are LiteRT or MediaPipe Tasks with a compatible TFLite model in app assets and CPU, GPU, or platform delegates; ONNX Runtime Mobile with an ONNX model and CPU, XNNPACK, NNAPI, or other execution providers; or ExecuTorch with an exported PyTorch program and a selected XNNPACK, Vulkan, Qualcomm, or other backend. iOS's native path is Core ML with an mlmodel or mlpackage, optionally wrapped by Vision; coremltools converts TensorFlow and PyTorch models, and current ML Program output targets iOS 15 or later. ONNX Runtime also supports iOS with Core ML and XNNPACK execution providers. Use separate detector, segmentation, and nutrition-database components rather than forcing a language model to produce authoritative nutrient numbers. Foodvisor's package proves CameraX capture, not a local inference runtime. device_requirements: Planning estimates for a new app, not measurements of Foodvisor: start with a quantized 20M-100M-parameter detector or segmenter, approximately 10-100 MB of model storage, about 0.5-1.5 GB of free process memory, and a target of roughly 50-200 ms for one still-photo inference on a recent A12-class iPhone or modern mid-range Android device with an accelerator. CPU fallback will be slower and use more battery. A 0.5B-3B or larger multimodal model typically needs hundreds of MB to multiple GB, int4 or int8 quantization, model download and cache controls, and device gating, so it should not be the baseline. Benchmark CPU, GPU, NPU or NNAPI/Core ML paths, app size, latency, thermal behavior, and battery on representative low, mid, and high tiers. The current Foodvisor App Store page reports a 277.8 MB app size and A12 requirement, but that is not evidence of model size. Sources: https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/tutorials/mobile/ ; https://developers.google.com/edge/mediapipe/solutions/vision/image_classifier/android ; https://apps.apple.com/us/app/foodvisor-ai-calorie-counter/id1064020872
expected_food_inference_quality: Evidence-backed expectations, not a Foodvisor benchmark: performance should be strongest when foods are separated, visible, well-lit, top-down, and common, matching Foodvisor's own capture guidance. Likely failure modes are mixed or occluded dishes, sauces and oils, hidden ingredients, culturally specific foods, visually similar items, brand and packaging variants, blur or glare, and exact portion mass. A single RGB photo cannot reliably see hidden ingredients or exact weight; autofocus or scale cues can add priors but cannot recover density or recipe composition. Foodvisor's correction workflow is important for these cases, and its terms disclaim accuracy and medical use. No independent current accuracy or portion-error benchmark for Foodvisor was found. privacy_and_compliance: Apple's privacy label says data linked to the user includes contact information, user and device identifiers, health and fitness data, purchases, photos or videos, product interaction, and customer support data; identifiers are listed for tracking and diagnostics are listed as not linked. Foodvisor's privacy PDF, updated 2025-11-18, describes diet, lifestyle, nutrition, and health processing, including allergies and medical history; it states one-year retention for connection logs and IP data, a maximum 13-month cookie period, EU hosting, and access or deletion requests through data@foodvisor.io. Its retention language is internally inconsistent: one section says health data is kept for service duration and immediately deleted on termination or account inactivity, while another summary says health data is retained until account deletion; the policy does not state a precise raw food-photo retention period. The terms grant Foodvisor a non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free license to use and modify uploaded food photos, allow partners or subprocessors as needed, mention encryption, say Apple Health data is used only when authorized and not for marketing or third-party sharing, and disclaim accuracy and medical use. Age eligibility wording should also be reconciled across the privacy policy and terms. For SuperNutrition, require granular photo and health consent, purpose limitation, short raw-image TTL, deletion and export, a subprocessor and DPA inventory, regional transfer safeguards, no model-training reuse without a separate opt-in, and eating-disorder and medical-claim safeguards. Sources: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/foodvisor-ai-calorie-counter/id1064020872 ; https://cdn.foodvisor.io/policies/fv_privacy_en.pdf ; https://www.foodvisor.io/en/terms-of-service/raw/
recommendation: Use a hybrid architecture for SuperNutrition: local quantized image-quality, orientation, and food-region detection or segmentation; a first-party backend that maps candidates to a controlled nutrition database; and an optional multimodal fallback for ambiguous cases. Transmit only after explicit consent, remove EXIF and unnecessary resolution, avoid raw-photo retention by default, return per-item confidence and uncertainty, and always provide edit, search, barcode, and manual fallback. For the next experiment, collect 300-500 consented representative meals with item and portion ground truth and compare a local detector, a cloud multimodal baseline, and a Foodvisor-like correction workflow on food recall, portion error, calorie error, correction rate, latency, battery, and retention. Do not infer Foodvisor's external provider from save_gpt_food or reproduce its endpoint; obtain runtime evidence or vendor disclosure if procurement depends on that attribution.
